records.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
records.summary:
Yogyakarta is among the eight provinces whose regional regulations OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined as discriminatory, and is one of the eight (with North Sumatra) for which no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people was documented in the dossier. The signal is legal divergence without operational evidence. Despite its special administrative status and cultural prominence, no trans-specific incident was found; the OutRight finding confirms a regulatory layer but does not demonstrate enforcement against visitors.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, the minimum reporting threshold; Yogyakarta shares this minimal-divergence tier with North Sumatra.

It sits above the operational-enforcement provinces (Aceh 0.03, West Java 0.08, West Sumatra 0.11) where raids, corporal punishment or enacted bylaws exist, below the capital territory (0.16) - also an OutRight focus province - and below Bali (0.22), which has no documented regulatory signal and benefits from tourism-economy tolerance.

records.name: Nothern Cape
records.summary:
The single documented trans-specific violent incident in this dossier occurred here: on 14 May 2024 in Upington, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was stabbed multiple times and her body set on fire in her own room, discovered by a family member who noticed the house burning. TGEU's Trans Day of Remembrance register records the killing and notes that "the LGBTIQ+ community in the Northern Cape has been shaken" - a province-level community response in a small province where one violent death is a meaningful rate observation. Police opened a murder case and reported no arrests at the time of the entry; the register records that police 'identified' the decedent by a deadname.

The killing is a lone incident and not clearly patterned or state-implicated; there is no evidence of impunity or victim-prosecution in the dossier, and no provincial legislative or enforcement finding against trans visitors. The score therefore reflects severity-dominant weighting: the method (burning) is extreme and the community-level shock signal is real, but the single-incident rule cautions against large score moves from an unpatterned crime. Northern Cape does not appear in the customary-authority / traditional-court geography and has no identified institutional climate finding.

records.name: Mpumalanga
records.summary:
Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.
